On Keeping Notes You Will Read Again

November 2023

Most notes are written once and read never. That is not a failure of discipline, and it is not solved by a better application. It is a failure of the moment of writing: the note was addressed to the person who had just finished reading, and that person no longer exists by the time anyone comes back to it. The reader who returns knows less than the writer did, and wants different things.

The fix is unglamorous. Write the note to someone who has forgotten the article. Say what the claim was, say why it mattered, and say what you would have to believe for it to be wrong. A note that carries all three survives being read cold, because it carries its own context instead of pointing at context that has evaporated.

What a note is for

A note is not a record of having read something. The record is the fact that the thing is in your library at all. A note is the one sentence you would say to a colleague who asked what was worth knowing, and most of the time writing it reveals that there was nothing. That is a useful thing to find out in thirty seconds rather than in six months.

There is a longer argument about this in reading things twice, which is really the same argument from the other side: if the note is good, the second reading is cheap, and if the note is bad, the second reading is the only thing that works.

What a note is for

The second time this heading appears is on purpose. Writers repeat themselves, and an outline that silently collapses two sections into one target sends a reader to the wrong half of the page. A table of contents has to be able to tell them apart even when their text is identical, which means the distinction cannot come from the words.

So the honest answer is that a note is for the version of you that has forgotten. Everything else — the tags, the folders, the bidirectional links — is an attempt to make forgetting survivable without doing the one thing that makes it survivable.
